title: Nusaybah bint Ka'b
hook: who fought at Uhud to shield the Prophet, and was praised by him

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ikrimah, son of Abu Jahl, greeted as a rider come home. Your line was welcomed like a traveler.

Wherever I turned, to the left or to the right, I saw her fighting to defend me. The early historians put those words in the mouth of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about a day when the lines broke and men ran. The one he saw was a woman of Medina. In the old accounts, she had come to the field to give water to the thirsty and tend the wounded. When the danger reached him, she set the water down and fought. Her name was Nusaybah bint Ka'b, also called Umm Umarah. Today: the woman who stayed when others ran.
screen: `LEFT OR RIGHT, I SAW HER.` → `SHE CAME WITH WATER.` → `SHE SET IT DOWN AND FOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Nusaybah was one of the helpers of Medina; the biographies place her among those who pledged themselves to the Prophet before he ever came to their city. The day of the broken lines was Uhud. As the early historians tell it, she fought beside her husband and her sons to keep attackers away from him, and she was wounded. Then come his words: left or right, wherever he turned, she was there. Not that she was strong for a woman. That she was there, every time he looked. These accounts come from the sira and the early biographical works, not from Bukhari, so they are told as the historians tell them. A second scene, in Tirmidhi, is brave in a different way. Umm Umarah came to the Prophet and said: I see that everything is for men, and I don't see women mentioned at all. A direct question, to his face. Tirmidhi reports that in answer a verse came down, the thirty-fifth of the surah called the Clans. It runs through the believers pair by pair: men who surrender and women who surrender, men who believe and women who believe, the truthful, the patient, the humble, the charitable, the fasting, men and women each time, ending with forgiveness and a great reward prepared for them all. So Nusaybah stood her ground twice: once on a hillside, with a sword, and once in a room, with a question. The Qur'an itself, reports say, answered the second.
screen: `A HELPER WHO PLEDGED EARLY.` · `THERE EVERY TIME HE LOOKED.` · `WHERE ARE THE WOMEN?` · `MEN AND WOMEN, PAIR BY PAIR.` · then, large: `SHE STOOD HER GROUND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one brave woman: a mother who held a family together, a nurse on a long night shift, a friend who asked the question nobody else would. See her clearly, say her name quietly, and hold what she did for a few breaths. If you pray, you can pray for her.
Nusaybah, also called Umm Umarah, who fought to defend the Prophet at Uhud when the lines broke, and later asked him where the women were in revelation. Today's word.
Your line: she stood her ground. On a hillside, and in a room. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims tell Nusaybah's story when they remember the women among the companions, and recite Surah al-Ahzab 33:35, which names believing men and women side by side.

notes: Uhud details (water, fighting beside husband and sons, wounds, the Prophet's praise) are from the sira/Tabaqat; framed as such. Confirm the attribution of the 'left or right' saying.
Her presence at the Aqabah pledge is from the sira; the script says 'the biographies place her among those who pledged'.
Tirmidhi 3211: confirm number and grading. Other reports (e.g. Ahmad, Nasa'i) attribute the question to Umm Salamah; noted in the trapdoor.
33:35 summarized, not quoted; Pickthall's wording was not used to avoid misquoting. Keeper may substitute the exact Pickthall text.
